summary: Explains what the IPFIX flow export protocol is good for, showing how different applications can use it and which information elements they would rely on. It also discusses the protocol's limits and how it relates to other measurement frameworks.

eli5.summary: IPFIX is like a tool that reports what traffic crosses a network. This note is the owner's guide: it says which jobs the tool suits, which it does not, and how it compares with other tools.

questions: can ipfix be used for billing
subtitle: What the IPFIX flow export protocol suits, where it falls short, and how it compares with other measurement frameworks.

tldr.problem: IPFIX is a general protocol for exporting IP flow information, but operators need to know which applications it fits and what it cannot do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, security, QoS monitoring and more, naming the Information Elements each needs. It then compares IPFIX with PSAMP, RMON, IPPM, AAA and RTFM and lists limitations.
tldr.outcome: IPFIX is a good fit for flow-based measurement, but as specified then it did not meet the reliability needed for usage-based billing and had no standard remote configuration.

today: RFC 5472 is an Informational RFC and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its limitation statements, such as the lack of standard remote configuration, describe IPFIX as of March 2009.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol defines how IP Flow information is exported from routers, measurement probes and other devices. It is a general data transport protocol that is easily extensible. This document shows how typical applications can use it, its opportunities and limits, and how it relates to other frameworks.

The examples use IPv4 only, but the statements apply to IPv4 and IPv6, and IPFIX has Information Elements (IEs) for both. IPFIX terms are defined in RFC 5101; the target applications and their requirements come from RFC 3917, and the standard IEs from RFC 5102.
sections.eli5: IPFIX is a way for network gear to send reports about the traffic it sees. This memo explains what those reports are good for.

sections.title: Applications of IPFIX
sections.content:
Accounting. Flows are defined by choosing the right keys, for example the five-value set of source address, destination address, protocol and two port numbers, or just the Diffserv codepoint and addresses for class-based accounting. The counters needed are packets and bytes per Flow, such as packetTotalCount and octetTotalCount.

Traffic profiling and engineering. Flow duration and volume, protocol and port distributions, and link utilization (by using interface IEs as keys) can all be derived. Using the same Flow Keys at all Observation Points makes records comparable. Neither RFC 5102 nor RFC 5477 defines IEs for exporting routing information.

Network security. Sudden load increases, many Flows to one destination, many ports or many hosts (a sign of port scanning), and an unusual ratio of TCP SYN to FIN packets (a sign of SYN flooding) can be spotted from Flow data. Capturing full packet traces everywhere is not viable because of resource limits and privacy concerns, so derived metrics, coarser Flows and sampling are suggested.

QoS monitoring. Per-packet metrics such as loss, delay and delay variation can be reported by treating a single packet as a Flow, using IEs from RFC 5477. Multi-point measurements need synchronized clocks and a way to recognize the same packet at two Observation Points, for example a hash-based packet ID carried in digestHashValue.
sections.eli5: Flow reports can be used to count who used how much, see what kinds of traffic are common, spot jammed roads, notice attacks, and measure how fast packets travel.

sections.title: A Worked Accounting Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of monitoring Flows in a Diffserv network against a service level agreement. Flows are distinguished by source and destination address, and the exported fields are sourceIPv4Address (4 octets), destinationIPv4Address (4 octets), ipDiffServCodePoint (1 octet) and octetDeltaCount (4 octets).

The Template set uses Set ID 2 and Template ID 256 with a field count of 4. The sample records use DSCP 46, the value recommended for Expedited Forwarding in RFC 3246, and example addresses from 192.0.2.0/24.
sections.eli5: First the sender announces the shape of its reports, like a form with four boxes. Then it sends filled-in forms, one per flow of traffic.

sections.title: IPFIX Compared with Other Frameworks
sections.content:
IPFIX runs over transports that work on IPv6 (SCTP, PR-SCTP, UDP or TCP), so it works in IPv4 and IPv6 networks without limitation. The RFC compares it with several other frameworks:

  • PSAMP exports packet records rather than Flow Records, builds on IPFIX, and addresses remote configuration through a MIB.
  • RMON exports through SNMP and MIBs. Its application performance transactions are service-oriented, while an IPFIX Flow simply groups packets by common properties.
  • IPPM metrics can be carried by IPFIX or computed from IPFIX data.
  • AAA and DIAMETER can be connected to an IPFIX Collector through a AAA client or an application specific module. This needs no change to IPFIX or DIAMETER, but the reliability limits still apply.
  • RTFM has a very similar architecture (meter, meter reader, manager) but uses SNMP, pull-mode collection, and bidirectional Flows. IPFIX pushes records, with SCTP and PR-SCTP mandatory and UDP and TCP optional, and encodes data more efficiently than SNMP.
sections.eli5: There are other tools that watch traffic. Some ask the network gear for numbers, while IPFIX makes the gear send reports on its own.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC is plain about what IPFIX does not do:

  • Not for billing-grade reliability. IPFIX does not support the record-loss resilience, fault tolerance, duplicate detection and application-layer acknowledgements that RFC 2975 requires for usage-based billing. Resilience to record loss is only possible with TCP or SCTP.
  • Transport. SCTP is the preferred protocol and a conforming implementation must work over it. Users need good reasons to use something else.
  • Push versus pull. Push suits export triggered by events at the Exporter, but makes export rate and resource use hard to predict. Pull suits requests from the Collector and protects it from overload.
  • Template IDs. IDs up to 255 are reserved for template and option sets, and 256 to 65535 go to data sets, so many Templates could exhaust the range.
  • Bidirectional Flows. The standard IEs describe one direction, and the workarounds either need agreed semantics or double the reporting of Flow Keys.
  • Remote configuration. There was no standard way to configure IPFIX processes remotely, though the RFC expected one soon.
sections.eli5: IPFIX is not a perfect bank-grade bookkeeper: reports can get lost, and there is no standard remote control yet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security requirements of RFC 3917 and RFC 5101 apply to all the scenarios. Using IPFIX for accounting or attack detection may raise the incentive to attack IPFIX itself. An attack that creates many Flows, for example with spoofed addresses, can overload Exporting and Collecting Processes, and flexible packet or Flow sampling can help. For inter-domain export, TLS or DTLS should be used.

Combining technologies can create new hazards: where a Collector or application specific module is a transit point to AAA, the security mechanisms, such as message encryption, must be maintained.
sections.eli5: Because the reports are valuable, bad guys may attack the reporting itself, so keep them private and do not let a flood of fake traffic drown the system.
